1:
Ellicott begins with the opening word: Now is only the simple illative and that heads all the historical books, marking the unity of the whole history but implying nothing of special connection in time or authorship with Samuel. The narrative, he adds, is hardly continuous, for it passes at once to the closing scene of David's life and leaves a comparative blank after the restoration that followed Absalom's defeat, which the later books partly fill.

On the king's age the witnesses are close but not agreed. Gill makes it exactly seventy, since David was thirty when he began to reign and reigned forty years, just the age of man. Clarke puts him at about sixty-nine, dying in his seventieth year, and dates these transactions about a year before his death. Ellicott says simply about seventy. Why a man of that age should be so broken they explain differently, and the explanations run moral, medical, biographical. Henry reads it as chastisement: David had been valiant and active, the flame always vehement in his breast, and now his blood is chilled and he is confined to his bed, punished for his former sins and especially the matter of Uriah, feeling hardships of his youth that he then made nothing of. Let not the strong man glory in his strength, Henry adds, and let the young remember their Creator before the evil days come. Clarke keeps to the body: sixty-nine is no great age, but David was exhausted by fatigues and family afflictions and older in constitution than in years, with wasting maladies to which the Psalms often refer. Ellicott combines both, that a life which took up its responsibilities early and was hard and trying throughout, and not wholly free from self-indulgence, reached complete decrepitude at no excessive age.

Ellicott notes that the clothes are bed-clothes, so the sense is that the king could no longer rise. Henry presses the futility of the remedy: clothes keep in an inward heat where there is any, but where there is none they have none to communicate, not even royal clothing. On the second remedy the sharpest disagreement falls. Clarke defends it as the best that could have been prescribed in such a state, the exhausted frame absorbing animal heat from a young and healthy body, and calls it Friar Bacon's secret for the cure of old age. Henry calls the physicians weak and unskilful, knowing no relief but outward applications, and the prescription foolish, nuptials for a man who should rather have been preparing for his funeral; they knew what would gratify their own corruptions, he says, and were willing enough to gratify his under colour of his health. His prophets should have been consulted as well as his physicians.

Abishag herself is placed by geography. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott agree that Shunem is the present Sulem or Solam, in Issachar and the plain of Jezreel, and Ellicott reports the conjecture that she is the fair Shulamite of the Song, which he thinks throws light on what follows in the next chapter. Both hold that the whole notice of her is introduced only for her later connection with the fate of Adonijah. That is also how Keil and Delitzsch account for the closing remark that the king knew her not: it is recorded neither to show David impotent nor to deny that she became his concubine, but to explain how Adonijah could afterwards ask for her as his wife, the affair being judged by the circumstances of a time when polygamy gave no offence. Henry agrees she was his secondary wife, married before he lay with her, which is why the request was imputed to Adonijah as a great crime. Clarke alone reads the words medically, by Bacon's maxim that one takes all one can from the medicine and gives nothing back, since to give is to increase the disease and hasten death.
5:
Adonijah's standing is settled first. Ellicott makes him David's fourth son, born in Hebron at least thirty-three years before, and gathers from Solomon's later words that he claimed the throne as now the eldest, Chileab having died as Amnon and Absalom had. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same place by another road: born after Absalom, he seemed once Absalom was dead to have the nearest claim. Clarke says only that he was evidently the eldest then living, and one of whom his father was particularly fond.

All three see Absalom behind the whole attempt. Ellicott lists the resemblances the narrative itself suggests, personal beauty, favour with a too-indulgent father, ambition and trust in popularity, and notes that the fifty runners, the chariots and horsemen, and the festal sacrifice with two great men of peace and war behind it are exactly imitated from that model; Clarke says flatly that he copied his brother in every respect. But Ellicott will not let the parallel flatter him. Adonijah shows little of the craft and ruthless determination of the elder rebel, and his attempt is crude and ill-planned in conception, wanting in promptitude of action.

On the father Henry does the chapter's closest reading. The text does not say the son never displeased his father, which he probably did often; it says the father never displeased the son, by crossing his humours, denying him anything he had a mind to, calling him to account, keeping him to his book or his business, or reproving what he saw amiss. David never asked him why he had done so, because he saw the question was uneasy to him. The fault was double: the son's, that he took reproof for an affront and so lost its benefit; the father's, that because it displeased him he did not reprove at all. Those who honour their sons more than God, he adds, forfeit the honour they might have expected from them. Gill puts the same charge shorter and harder, that in this David was guilty of the same sin as Eli, and that Adonijah presumed upon it. Keil and Delitzsch call it weak oversight, and say it encouraged the attempt.

Why Joab and Abiathar joined him is asked by three and answered differently by each. Gill looks at their offices and temper: the one was general and had the soldiery, the other high priest with a share in the affections of the people, whose office it was to anoint a king, and Adonijah applied to them knowing them to be on some accounts discontented. Keil and Delitzsch give Joab a motive, that he had fallen out with David and hoped to secure his influence under a king he had helped to the throne, but confess they do not know what moved Abiathar, unless jealousy of Zadok and fear of being thrown further into the shade. Henry refuses a motive and finds the thing a wonder: old men faithful through David's hardest times, men of sense not easily wheedled, already at the top of their preferment with nothing to gain and every interest in obliging Solomon; God left them to themselves, perhaps to correct them for some former misconduct with a scourge of their own making.

Whether the meal was a sacrifice divides them. Clarke holds that with Abiathar present the animals were undoubtedly offered sacrificially and the guests fed on the victims, so that he gave a popular colour to his pretensions by affecting to receive his authority from God; Keil and Delitzsch likewise call it a solemn sacrificial meal at which he was proclaimed. Gill makes it a banquet only, large and elegant for a numerous party. Henry reports the sacrificial reading as the opinion of some, and draws the moral that all religious exercises should not be made to patronise irreligious practices.
11:
Nathan moves first, and Ellicott finds that natural: he had been the medium both of the promise of a son who should build the house and of the blessing embodied in the name Jedidiah, and perhaps for that reason the conspirators held aloof from him altogether. Henry notes who did not know. David knew nothing, for disobedient children think themselves well off if they can keep a good old parent ignorant, though a bird of the air will carry the voice; Bathsheba lived retired and knew nothing either, and many get through this world comfortably who know little how it goes; Solomon probably knew and was as a deaf man that heard not, leaving the matter to God and his friends, so that David could say in his psalm for Solomon that while men rise early and sit up late in vain, God giveth his beloved sleep.

Whose life was actually at stake they do not agree. Keil and Delitzsch say that had Adonijah got possession he would have put Solomon and his mother out of the way, by the barbarous custom of the East, as political opponents; Clarke assumes the same and breaks out against the cursed lust of rule, by which a father will destroy his son, a son depose his father, and a brother murder a brother to obtain a crown. Ellicott is cooler: the usurpation would of course be sealed with the blood of the rival Solomon, but Bathsheba need hardly have been sacrificed, except that her position of favour would excite jealousy and Solomon, being young, might be thought only an instrument in her hands.

The oath she pleads is nowhere else on record, and both critics say so. Clarke thinks it very likely made, and known only to Bathsheba and Nathan. Ellicott suggests it may belong to Solomon's birth, and points to a designation in Chronicles apparently earlier, it being understood by Oriental custom that such a choice, without strict regard to priority of birth, lay with the reigning king.

That opens the chapter's constitutional question, and three answers are given. Clarke states it as a fact of the case: this was a monarchy neither hereditary nor elective, for the king simply named his successor, and he adds, having examined both systems, that hereditary monarchy carries a high balance of evidence over the elective and is every way safer for the state and more secure for the subject. Ellicott grounds it in custom, the prerogative of the reigning king. Henry grounds it in prophecy, and refuses the other footing outright: the eyes of all Israel were on David not as a king, since it is no prerogative of any prince to bequeath his subjects by will as though they were his goods and chattels, but as a prophet, for all Israel knew the Spirit of the Lord spoke by him, and therefore his word in a matter of such importance would be an oracle and a law.

Henry also reads Bathsheba's conduct closely. She came on Esther's errand, to intercede for her life, though needing no call as Esther did; she found Abishag ministering and took no displeasure; she bowed in respect to David both as prince and husband. Her address was discreet in four steps, the oath first, because that would hold so conscientious a man fast, then the news he had not heard, with the excusing clause that the fault was not his since he knew nothing, then the observation that Solomon alone was uninvited, no oversight but a contempt of the settlement, and last the danger, that usurpers are cruel and Adonijah would not have dealt with Solomon as Solomon afterwards dealt with him. Ellicott marks a change of manner in all this, a growth of court ceremony since Absalom's defeat, so that entering the bedchamber is an intrusion to be ventured only as a suppliant.
22:
Nathan comes in while Bathsheba is still speaking, and Henry takes the timing to be the point: he seconded her before the king could answer, lest hearing only her representation David should be dilatory and say he would consider of it, whereas out of the mouth of two such witnesses the word would be established and orders follow at once. Gill notices the pretence kept up, Nathan telling his story as though he knew nothing of her application and the king had never heard of the matter. Henry observes that he paid the same reverence finding the king sick in bed as on his throne, bowing with his face to the ground, yet dealt more plainly than Bathsheba had, which his character would bear and the king's low spirits made necessary.

The question he puts, whether David had said that Adonijah should reign, is read two ways. Ellicott takes it as merely drawing out a denial, and finds it true to nature that it does so by assuming, as court language would, that nothing of the kind could be conceived as done without the king's will; and he marks the contrast between Nathan so deferential on business of state and the bold superiority of his tone in his true prophetic office. Henry makes it a dilemma with three limbs: if the thing were David's doing he was not so faithful to God's word or his own as all had taken him to be; if it were not, it was high time to witness against the usurpation; and if he knew nothing of it, what daring insolence was in Adonijah and his party. Good men would do their duty if they were reminded of it, Henry adds, and those who act as their remembrancers do them a real kindness.

Clarke alone attends to the procedure. Bathsheba had gone out when Nathan came in, and he withdrew when she was called back, so each had a separate audience; and to Nathan, he notes, the king expressed no will at all. Gill marks the geography of the report, that Adonijah had gone down from Jerusalem, which lay high, to the stone of Zoheleth in the valley.

On the oath Henry dwells. David repeats the promise and oath he had made, and though old and his memory beginning to fail he remembers this, an oath being so sacred that its obligation cannot be broken and so solemn that its impression cannot be forgotten. He then ratifies it with another, as the Lord liveth that hath redeemed my soul out of all distress, which Henry takes for his usual form on solemn occasions and a grateful acknowledgment of the goodness that brought him through all the hardships in his way, mentioned now to God's glory as Jacob did when dying, and perhaps to encourage his son in distresses of his own. Dying saints ought to be witnesses for God and speak of him as they have found him. Ellicott calls the same adjuration characteristic of David but peculiarly appropriate in an old man so near the haven of rest after all the storms of life.

The closing blessing divides them in a smaller way. Keil and Delitzsch report that she withdrew with the deepest prostration and a blessing out of her inmost gratitude, and add that the formula, may the king live for ever, was used by Israelites only on occasions of special importance, while Babylonians and ancient Persians addressed their kings so constantly. Ellicott flattens it, noting that the words are literally only may the king live, the very acclamation given to Adonijah at the feast. Henry takes it at full weight: so far was she from thinking that David had lived too long that she prayed he might live for ever if it were possible, and we should desire the prolonging of useful lives however it postpones advantages of our own.
32:
Ellicott opens on the change in David. This sudden flash of the old energy, and the terse directions he gives for every part of the inauguration, are striking in themselves and more so against the despondency with which, far younger, he had taken the news of Absalom's rebellion; then he felt a threatened chastisement coming, and now he knows it past and God on his side.

The mule carries more weight than it looks. Keil and Delitzsch explain that when the king let a man ride the beast he rode himself it was a sign of succession, and compare the Persian honour of riding the king's horse. Clarke puts it as law rather than sign: no subject could use anything belonging to the prince without forfeiting his life, so the mule was full evidence that David had appointed his heir. Gill draws a different inference, reporting that the Jews gather from the servants of your lord that a king stands above a high priest, since David calls himself lord of Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet.

Two then analyse the ceremony and arrive independently at the same shape. Ellicott notices the completeness of the old king's provision: riding the royal mule attended by the body-guard marked the royal sanction, the anointing the sanction of priest and prophet, the acclamation the adhesion of the people, with enthronement and homage to follow. Clarke sets out the same four steps, adding that the king elect was taken to a public well or river where the concourse was greatest so all might see who was appointed, and that the continual stream at Gihon denoted the kingdom's perpetuity. Ellicott doubts where Gihon lay, west near the present Jaffa gate or more probably south at the end of the valley running through the city, and notes the Targums read Siloam, which suits the second guess and the nearness of Adonijah's feast.

Why anoint at all is answered the same way twice. Keil and Delitzsch report the unanimous opinion of the Rabbins that where the succession was unquestioned there was no anointing at all, and hold it needed here because Adonijah's attempt had made the title doubtful while the old king lived. Henry reasons from Solomon's position, no first of his line as Saul and David were but a younger son made king by divine appointment against a contested claim, so the unction settled it. Henry turns the point against the usurper: we do not find that Abiathar pretended to anoint Adonijah, who was made king by a feast and not by an unction, and whom God calls he will qualify.

Where the oil came from they agree against a rabbi. Gill holds it came from the tent David had pitched for the ark, not the tabernacle at Gibeon, too far off when haste was required, and reports but disapproves Kimchi's view that it stood at Gibeon and was fetched thence. Keil and Delitzsch say the same, and Ellicott adds the awkwardness that haste forced the nearer source although Abiathar presided in Zion and Zadok only at Gibeon.

On Benaiah's answer Keil and Delitzsch defend him against the charge of flattering a father's vanity, holding that the wish for a throne greater than David's had the prosperity of the monarchy in view and was granted. Henry says the wisest and best man desires his children to be wiser and better than himself. Clarke, more worldly, observes that such a wish is borne from a son but is no compliment in ordinary cases, since it seems to insinuate a reflection on the father, and he quotes a Latin panegyrist whose words to an emperor run close to Benaiah's. Ellicott reads the shouting that follows as more than conventional loyalty, and draws the political conclusion: Adonijah had the great men and perhaps the army, but no popular following at all.
41:
It is Joab who hears it. Ellicott calls it one of the narrative's life-like touches that amid the revelry it is the old warrior who catches the trumpet and the shouting after it, while Adonijah affects to disregard it; Keil and Delitzsch add that the sound carried to the fountain of Rogel, and that in hailing Jonathan as a brave man with good tidings Adonijah was suppressing his anxiety, knowing both his father's mind about the succession and how powerful Solomon's friends were. Henry reads the length of the dinner as evidence: the whole business of the anointing was finished while they sat glutting themselves, which shows how secure they felt. Usurpers flatter themselves with hopes of success, he adds, and those are least timorous whose condition is most dangerous; how can men who do evil deeds expect good tidings, when the worthiest man brings them the worst news?

Clarke sets out Jonathan's four points as the messenger gave them: the nomination, the three men appointed, the ride to Gihon and anointing, and the enthronement. Ellicott recalls him named before with Ahimaaz as a swift runner fit for a messenger. Keil and Delitzsch catch his opening word, an assurance with a slight doubt in it, and note that the thrice repeated and also raises the account towards certainty. Clarke, who thinks him an observer if not a spy, cannot tell how he came by so much information so fast.

Henry lingers on the servants' blessing, that God would make Solomon's name better than his father's, which it might well be with his father's foundation to build on, for a child on a giant's shoulders is higher than the giant. Ellicott notes the king bowed in worship, joining their prayer and thanking God for a promise fulfilled.

The collapse they explain three ways. Gill observes that many guests were military men, the general and his captains, who had they taken to arms would have given Solomon much trouble, and concludes the panic was no doubt of God. Ellicott finds nothing more striking than so humiliating a collapse in a plot supported by Joab and Abiathar, set against Absalom's formidable rebellion, and takes it for evidence that the royal power had been consolidated in David's last peaceful years, the attempt being seen not as rebellion against David but as presumption on his favour, and so falling at a word from him. He adds a puzzle: of all the conspirators Adonijah alone seems to have feared punishment, while his accomplices disperse in safety and their rebellion is ignored. Henry only says the triumphing of the wicked is short, and they had built a castle in the air.

At the altar the commentary turns legal. Ellicott explains that the horns were projections to which victims were fastened and on which blood was sprinkled, so that to grasp them was to claim sanctuary, a right the Law denied to wilful murder and later refused to Joab; Adonijah, by calling him King Solomon, seems to plead his usurpation as one of those acts of haste to which alone sanctuary was conceded. Clarke says the altar was a privileged place and to molest a man there was reckoned sacrilege. Henry presses the irony that one who had despised Solomon as not worth inviting now dreads him as his judge, and that men who slight the altar in security catch at its horns too late.

What the sentence meant divides them. Keil and Delitzsch hold that go to thy house does not banish him from court, Solomon being unwilling to begin his reign with a punishment and granting life on condition of quiet. Clarke reads the same words as excluding him from any place about the king's person or under the government. Ellicott calls the pardon extraordinary grace by Oriental measure, yet cautious and conditional, withdrawn at the first symptom of a renewed claim.
